summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app I use myself, and this month the work has mostly been about catching the gap between "the app looks like it's teaching" and it actually teaching.

The core bug: the practice engine gated content on whether I could read the script, but never checked whether I'd actually been told what a word means. It broke on the clock drill — I got asked "it is seven o'clock" in Japanese before I'd ever seen the word for seven. My comprehension score on that lesson was 2 out of 10, and it wasn't because the material was hard, it was because the material had never been taught. The fix was a precondition I hadn't modeled: read-the-script, met-the-word, and allowed-to-produce-the-word turned out to be three separate gates, not one.

A similar shape showed up in the image generation. I switched the art style from generic anime to something that reads better for an adult learner, and along the way found that image models can't count — ask for "seven balls in two rows" and you get six, or nine, or twelve, never seven. The fix wasn't a smarter prompt, it was giving the model a shape instead of an arithmetic fact ("one straight row of seven" works because there's nothing to round to a symmetric grid). For the clock-time cards specifically I ended up not generating images at all — I composited a marker onto clock faces I'd already reviewed, because a generated card can silently drift from its neighbors and nobody would notice until a student did.

The grammar engine also didn't have a verb for most of its life — sentences were just fixed templates with a noun slot, which is fine for beginner material but caps out fast. Adding real verb conjugation meant every downstream piece (which sentences are "the same grammar point," how quiz distractors get picked, how English translations render) had to stop assuming one fixed sentence shape. The interesting failure along the way: a multiple-choice comprehension quiz was scoring 88% correct, which sounded good until I noticed the four answer choices in English gave away the answer without needing to read the Japanese at all — flipping the direction (English prompt, Japanese answer tiles) dropped the "solvable without reading" rate to zero, which is what the score was supposed to mean in the first place.
